title: OpenAI’s answer to Meta Muse is a cute AI agent that never clocks out
summary: The always-on AI agents can keep projects moving across your apps while you’re away.
body: TL;DR OpenAI’s new Dots are always-on AI agents that can keep working across connected apps even when you’re not actively chatting with them. A Dot can monitor ongoing work, suggest or complete next steps, and carry context across ChatGPT, Slack, and Teams. Dots are rolling out gradually to Pro, Business Premium, and Enterprise users in eligible markets. ChatGPT began as a place you opened when you needed an answer. Then ChatGPT Work pushed things further, taking on long-running jobs across apps and files. OpenAI’s next step is to make the AI stick around even after you close the chat. At DevDay 2026, the company unveiled Dots , always-on personal agents that can keep working toward your goals in the background. Powered by GPT-6 Astra , each Dot gets its own cloud computer and browser and can connect to more than 4,000 apps through OpenAI’s plugin ecosystem. OpenAI dresses them up as colorful, fuzzy characters you can name, but the idea goes deeper than a mascot. You can talk or message your Dot through ChatGPT, then reach the same agent through Slack or Microsoft Teams without losing context. Texting is coming soon.

DevDay is here for OpenAI, and that means the company is sharing a whole bunch of news about its latest work on models and the services built around them. While we just heard that GPT-6.1 Astra is getting sent back to the bench for misbehaving, progress continues on the rest of OpenAI’s headlining models, and this afternoon we’re getting the scoop on the first member of that 6.1-series to actually make its public debut, with the launch of GPT‑6.1 Sol. While we only just got GPT-6 Sol , OpenAI is not a company to rest on its laurels, and today is pushing right on forward with the evolution of GPT-6.1 Sol . Even though Astra remains the more capable model, with these 6.1 improvements, OpenAI reports that Sol is rapidly approaching Astra in “intelligence,” nearly matching the flagship model in performance across multiple metrics.

title: Your next Google Play subscription could work very differently
summary: New tools also add bundles, team seats, and smarter payment recovery.
body: TL;DR Google Play is adding usage-based subscription billing aimed at AI apps and other services with variable costs. New options will also support team subscriptions, mixed subscription/one-time purchases, and cross-app bundles. Google is also testing smarter grace periods, cancellation discounts, cheaper-plan offers, and Play Store winback deals. Google Play’s billing story changed earlier this year when Google opened the door wider to alternative billing systems and external web payments, giving Android users more choice over how they pay. Now it is turning its attention to subscriptions that still run through Google Play itself, with new billing options that could make AI apps, bundles, and failed payments work very differently for users. In a blog post , Google says it is testing and rolling out several new subscription options, including Usage-Based Billing. The new system targets services with variable costs, such as generative AI apps , and it lets users maintain a prepaid balance that can automatically top up when it drops below a set threshold. That opens the door to billing tied to consumption rather than only a fixed recurring amount.

title: ChatGPT’s $200 Pro plan is finally coming back, but OpenAI is changing the deal
summary: The returning tier gets new usage math as an even pricier option surfaces.
body: TL;DR OpenAI is reopening new subscriptions to its $200 ChatGPT Pro plan on September 30 after pausing them earlier this month. The returning plan offers about half the previous API-dollar allowance, though OpenAI says cheaper models and the removal of the five-hour cap should offset it. Meanwhile, an unannounced $500/month ChatGPT Pro Max tier has surfaced, promising the “Fastest Work and Codex” as a key perk. For nearly three weeks, anyone who wanted ChatGPT’s most expensive individual plan had to wait on the sidelines. OpenAI paused new sign-ups for its $200 Pro tier on September 10 after unprecedented demand for GPT-6 Astra , leaving the $100 Pro option as the highest plan newcomers could actually buy. That wait is about to end, but the returning $200 plan won’t work exactly like the one that disappeared. OpenAI’s Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux says new subscriptions to the $200 Pro plan will reopen on September 30. The price stays the same, but OpenAI is changing how it calculates usage. Sottiaux says the new allowance works out to roughly half the “API spend” of the previous $200 plan.

title: Thousands of iOS apps started crashing because of Google (wait, what?)
summary: One small bug for Google, one giant pain for developers.
body: TL;DR A bug in Google Analytics for Firebase caused thousands of iOS apps to start crashing. Google resolved the bug in a couple of hours, but the crashes have continued for several hours due to caching. Some apps saw crash numbers over 5,000 times higher than normal. App crashes aren’t new, but they usually happen with new software versions , new smartphones , or app updates. They are also usually fairly limited in scope. However, Google’s Firebase SDK reportedly experienced an issue a few hours ago that was catastrophic enough to crash thousands of iOS apps and send unsuspecting developers into a frenzy. According to a now-resolved thread on the Google Firebase GitHub issue tracker, a problem in Google Analytics for Firebase iOS caused apps to crash at launch. Since thousands of apps rely on Firebase for backend development and analytics, they all started crashing around the same time, sparking a flurry of panicked posts from developers wondering what had happened.

body: TL;DR OpenAI has reportedly canceled plans to launch GPT-6.1 Astra due to safety concerns. The model didn’t follow instructions during internal testing, per reports. It also tried to deceive OpenAI researchers and perform actions beyond the scope of its assigned tasks. OpenAI has been releasing new models at breakneck speed. It launched GPT-6 Astra earlier this month and followed it up with new GPT-6 Sol and Luna models last week. It seems the company was gearing up to launch a new GPT-6.1 Astra model, only to have a wrench thrown into its plans. According to a report from The Wall Street Journal , OpenAI has canceled plans to launch GPT-6.1 Astra due to safety concerns. GPT-6.1 Astra was expected to be a major improvement over the already impressive GPT-6 Astra, especially in terms of handling tasks without human assistance. However, OpenAI’s researchers raised security concerns during internal testing of the new model.

title: This long-anticipated Google Recorder feature is live for Pixel users
summary: The recently leaked ‘Access recording in other apps’ toggle is now available on Google Recorder.
body: TL;DR The Google Recorder app’s “Allow recordings in other apps” toggle is now rolling out to Pixel users. This toggle is enabled by default, and all your existing audio files will appear in a folder named Recordings in the file manager app of your choice. We first discovered this toggle last week, and it’s already appearing in the latest version of the audio recording app. When it comes to audio recording apps, the Pixel-exclusive Google Recorder covers all the bases. It can automatically transcribe your audio files and cleverly sync them to the cloud for easier access across devices. However, because recordings are sandboxed away from the rest of your storage, file manager apps can’t access them. Fortunately, we knew this could change soon , and that day is finally here. With the release of Recorder version 4.2.20260823 last week, Google appears to have quietly enabled the “Allow recordings in other apps” toggle within the app’s settings page.

title: This Meta Muse incident is a scary warning about trusting AI agents
summary: Convenience is great, until your AI starts making the arrangements.
body: TL;DR Meta’s Muse negotiated a Facebook Marketplace sale, shared the seller’s address, and arranged a pickup without him realizing someone was coming. Meta is investigating the incident, and it remains unclear whether Muse overstepped its permissions or acted on authorization it had already received. The incident highlights the risks of handing sensitive, real-world decisions to AI agents, especially when personal information or in-person interactions are involved. It’s only been a few days since Meta launched Muse, and we’re already getting a sense of how much Meta wants its new AI agent to do . But the more an AI can do for you, the more you also have to trust it with. One early Muse experience shows why that can get uncomfortable very quickly. Threads user Matt Robb shared what happened after using Muse to handle a Facebook Marketplace listing. According to screenshots he posted, the AI negotiated with a buyer, agreed to a price, shared his address, and arranged a pickup — all without him realizing someone had actually been invited over.
